v: Know why Japanese has three writing systems
Understand what you actually need to learn

b.v: Japanese is written with three sets of characters at the same time. This sounds worse than it is — each has a clear job.

v: ひらがな hiragana = the 46 basic sounds, used for Japanese words and grammar
カタカナ katakana = the same 46 sounds, used for foreign words and names
漢字 kanji = Chinese characters, each carrying a meaning

b.v: Hiragana comes first. Everything can be written in hiragana, and every learner starts there.
2) The vowels — only five, and they never change

v: あ a — like the a in father
い i — like ee in see
う u — like oo in food, but with flat lips
え e — like e in bed
お o — like o in cold

b.v: Japanese vowels are always these five sounds. Unlike English, a is never 'ay' and e is never 'ee'. Once you learn them, every word is readable.
Every other row is a consonant plus those same five vowels.

v: Write the five vowels five times each, saying them out loud
Read these without help: あお, ここ, かき
さ sa  し shi  す su  せ se  そ so
た ta  ち chi  つ tsu  て te  と to
な na  に ni  ぬ nu  ね ne  の no
は ha  ひ hi  ふ fu  へ he  ほ ho
ま ma  み mi  む mu  め me  も mo
や ya       ゆ yu       よ yo
ら ra  り ri  る ru  れ re  ろ ro

b.v: Notice し is shi not si, ち is chi not ti, and つ is tsu not tu. These three are the only surprises in the whole set.
A pair of small strokes or a small circle changes the consonant. This is not new characters to learn — it is the same ones with a mark.

v: は ha → ぱ pa (small circle)

b.v: 3) ん is the only lone consonant
Every other character is a whole syllable. ん is the single exception — an n on its own, and it is always counted as a full beat.

v: Read each row out loud, three times
Read these: なまえ, にほん, ともだち
Do not try to memorise all 46 today. Read them daily and they stick in a week.
Greet at any time of day
おはようございます = ohayou gozaimasu = good morning (polite)
こんにちは = konnichiwa = hello / good afternoon
こんばんは = konbanwa = good evening
おやすみなさい = oyasuminasai = good night

b.v: こんにちは is written with は but pronounced wa. Same with こんばんは. This is a leftover from old grammar.

v: ありがとうございます = arigatou gozaimasu = thank you (polite)
すみません = sumimasen = excuse me / sorry / thank you
ごめんなさい = gomen nasai = I am sorry

b.v: すみません does three jobs: getting attention, apologising, and thanking someone for trouble taken. It is probably the most used word in Japan.

v: はじめまして = hajimemashite = how do you do (first meeting only)
よろしくおねがいします = yoroshiku onegaishimasu = please treat me well
さようなら = sayounara = goodbye (formal, or a long parting)
じゃあね = jaa ne = see you (casual)
お先に失礌します = osaki ni shitsurei shimasu = excuse me for leaving first

b.v: よろしくおねがいします has no English equivalent. It is said when meeting someone, starting work together, or asking a favour — roughly 'I am in your care'.

v: Introduce yourself: はじめまして、よろしくおねがいします
Say your name and where you are from
Ask the same of someone else

b.v: Japanese marks the topic with は (written ha, said wa) and ends with です, which does the job of 'is' or 'am'.

v: わたしはカリドです = watashi wa Khalid desu = I am Khalid
です = desu = am / is / are (polite)

b.v: Your name goes in katakana, because it is a foreign word. カリド is Khalid.

v: パキスタンから来ました = Pakisutan kara kimashita = I came from Pakistan
お名前は？ = onamae wa? = what is your name?
どこから来ましたか？ = doko kara kimashita ka? = where did you come from?
か = ka = turns any sentence into a question

b.v: か at the end is the whole question mark. 学生です is 'I am a student'. 学生ですか is 'are you a student?'.
Never call someone by their bare name. Add さん (san) — Tanaka-san. Never add it to your own name.
Say the whole thing with your own details:

v: はじめまして。わたしは ___ です。___ から来ました。よろしくおねがいします。
Understand why counting is different in Japanese

b.v: 4 and 7 have two readings each. よん and なな are safer — し (shi) also means death, so it is often avoided.
2) Above ten it is simple arithmetic
3) Counters — the part that surprises people
Japanese cannot count things with numbers alone. A small word goes after the number, and which one depends on the shape of the thing.

v: 人 nin — people: 三人 san-nin = three people
本 hon — long thin things: ペン二本 pen ni-hon = two pens
枚 mai — flat things: 切符三枚 kippu san-mai = three tickets
つ tsu — the general one, works when you do not know: 一つ hitotsu = one thing

b.v: When stuck, use つ with the native numbers: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ. Everyone understands, and it is never wrong enough to matter.

v: いくらですか？ = ikura desu ka? = how much is it?
Count three people, three pens, three tickets
Understand why the verb comes last
Learn the four particles that matter most

b.v: About 30 minutes. This is the lesson that makes Japanese click.
1) The verb goes at the end
English is subject-verb-object: 'I eat sushi'. Japanese is subject-object-verb: 'I sushi eat'. Once you expect it, it stops feeling backwards.

v: わたしはすしをたべます = watashi wa sushi wo tabemasu = I eat sushi

b.v: 2) Particles mark the job of each word
Japanese does not rely on word order to say who did what. Small words after each noun do that job — which is why the order can move around.

v: は wa — the topic: わたしは = as for me
を wo — the object: すしを = sushi (the thing being eaten)
に ni — to, at, in a time: 三時に = at three o'clock
で de — at, by means of: 学校で = at school

b.v: 3) は and が — the classic difficulty
は marks what the sentence is about. が points at the subject, often when it is new information or the answer to a question. Do not expect to master this now — nobody does in a week.
4) Polite verbs end in ます

v: たべます → たべません tabemasen = do not eat
たべます → たべました tabemashita = ate
たべませんでした tabemasendeshita = did not eat

b.v: This is beautifully regular. Learn the four endings once and every polite verb follows them.

v: Make five sentences: I eat, I drink, I go, I see, I do
Turn each one negative, then past
パン pan = bread — from Portuguese, so it is katakana
やきとり yakitori = grilled chicken skewers
おでん oden = simmered winter dish
カレー karee = curry, Japanese style
すみません = sumimasen = excuse me (this is how you call a waiter)
これをください = kore wo kudasai = this one, please
メニューをください = menyuu wo kudasai = menu, please
お水をください = omizu wo kudasai = water, please
お会計お願いします = okaikei onegaishimasu = the bill, please

b.v: ください kudasai means 'please give me'. Put any noun plus を in front of it and you can order almost anything.

v: 豚肉はたべません = butaniku wa tabemasen = I do not eat pork
ベジタリアンです = bejitarian desu = I am vegetarian
おいしいです = oishii desu = it is delicious
いただきます = itadakimasu = said before eating
ごちそうさまでした = gochisousama deshita = said after eating

b.v: Order a meal out loud: call the waiter, ask for the menu, order one dish and water, ask for the bill.

v: そこ soko = there, near you

b.v: Notice the pattern: ko- is near me, so- is near you, a- is far from both, do- is the question. This runs through the whole language — これ, それ, あれ, どれ.

v: トイレはどこですか？ = toire wa doko desu ka? = where is the toilet?
駅はどこですか？ = eki wa doko desu ka? = where is the station?
これは何ですか？ = kore wa nan desu ka? = what is this?
コンビニ konbini = convenience store
まっすぐ massugu = straight ahead
東京までの切符をください = a ticket to Tokyo, please
何時ですか？ = nanji desu ka? = what time is it?

v: 三時半 sanji-han = half past three

b.v: Katakana has the same 46 sounds as hiragana but different shapes. It is used for foreign words, names, and sometimes emphasis — like italics.

v: ア a  イ i  ウ u  エ e  オ o
カ ka  キ ki  ク ku  ケ ke  コ ko

b.v: The long dash ー stretches the vowel. コーヒー is koo-hii, not ko-hi.
